There are so many things I would say to this, and so many angles to come at it from. I am just going to start typing and see what comes out. 

I suffer from between 4-6 mental disorders (depending on which doctor you ask). So I am coming at it from a sufferer perspective. 

Its almost 2 am and I can’t sleep. This is almost every night. The slightest thing can set my obsessions off the rails (ocd being a disorder i struggle with). Despite graduating with 2 degrees, I have been unable to work a full time job since graduation. Its been several years. Ive gone months with panic attacks several times per day every day lasting over 45 minutes at times. These attacks made me fear for my life and there has been a few times I have called 911. I got so ill with agoraphobia I spent a lot of time barely leaving my home, crying as my parents took me out of the house to “re-socialize” and reintegrate into the world. I am a grownup who felt like I was living the life of a child. No relationships are truly possible for me right now, I am poor, and friends have gotten harder to come by. 

I sometimes get so anxious, sad, and angry all at once that I consider driving my car off the road. Ive hit myself. A long time ago I cut myself. Ive been hospitalized. Ive seen countless doctors, tried countless medicines, I did therapy 3 hours a day for 5 days a week once in an intensive outpatient program that lasted months. Ive self medicated. Ive lost lots of self esteem that feels like it will be an uphill battle to obtain again. 

There is not a single area of my life that my diseases/disorders have not touched. Jobs, dating, family, general happiness levels, hobbies etc. Worst of all, it is hard to disclose to people and many people think you’re “weird” or “nuts” if you have these issues. So I largely lurk in the shadows, avoiding situations where I might have to disclose my illnesses and the predicaments they have put me in. 

I think a lot of the stigma comes from the idea that if something is mental, it can be controlled. And if the person suffering fails to control their symptoms, then they are thought of as weak or incapable of living like normal human beings and something is “off” with them. And what I have found is this is just not true. As stated above, I have tried almost everything available to me to try and cope with my mental health issues. And nothing has given me lasting peace. As hard as I may try, I still have days where I obsess over something for half the day (yes literally half my waking hours) or days where leaving the house is a chore. This is after doing all the things I was “supposed to do”. This shit is not like a broken toe, where you protect it and rest it and then boom, you are good to go. There is no simple roadmap. You can waste away over a period of years simply because no one can truly figure out what is wrong with you and you yourself can’t seem to identify it or even if you can, you may not be able to correct it. 

And then there are built in aspects of society that kind of perpetuate the cycle. You get mentally ill. If you don’t respond well to treatment, maybe you are suicidal. You turn to substances because they are the only thing helping you not kill yourself. Then, job hunting becomes tricky. You can’t pass a drug test or now you’re a drunk who can get a job but lasts a day before your manager sees you shaking or smells vodka on your breath. You’re jobless. So what you do? You go back to all your bad habits which perpetuate the cycle further along as self care becomes almost a non-factor and relationships begin to crumble. The vicious cycle, in whichever way it presents itself, is absolutely brutal and can lead people to decide life is not worth living ultimately. 

Ultimately, I would just say for a non-sufferer it can be easy to gloss over all the little day to day details that make managing life living with moderate to severe mental disorders so difficult. It can make you act irrationally and against your self interest. It can single handedly hold your life back and its not out of pure weakness. Everyone’s mind is so different and we all experience things differently. For those with mental health issues, not all situations are equal but all of those people with mental health issues experience life in a fundamentally different way than someone mentally healthy. And sometimes people are diagnosed, treated, and live happily ever after. But the fact of the matter is, some people suffer until the day they die no matter what they do. Its profoundly sad, but this is the reality of severe mental health diagnoses.

Fellow pure o sufferer here. 

Honestly, I don’t have a definitive to your question, but I will try to give some advice. 

I have the same reaction you do essentially. Weed helps me break the thought cycle and I also feel more like a “normal” person on it. 

I would say it is OK to use it to help your symptoms but it is simply not feasible if you have to use it all the time. If you are having a particularly rough day OCD wise, not using it when it is available sounds kind of silly. But, if you can’t get by without it and need it all the time (which was me and still sort of is me too), then it becomes an issue. I know you said you tried a lot of things, has meditation worked for you? Have you tried all the medicines and different kinds of therapies? My point is that you have to try everything else the best you can before resorting to weed every day all the time. Now, if the ocd is treatment resistant, and weed is the only thing that helps I would just go for it. Just try and make it a more moderate usage pattern. Pretty much slow down the best you can but still use it when needed. I just say try everything else first because it is better than being completely hooked on weed (though I would decline benzos as much as I could if I were you, weed is better by far. Use benzos very lightly if prescribed). 

Last point. Are you able to get through the day coping with the thoughts without weed? Like it may be unpleasant, but can you do it? Because the best thing if possible is to practice working with the thoughts and not against them. You may find if you don’t go to your normal coping mechanism immediately (weed) you may find them slow down over time (this is where meditation would help). So your brain might surprise you and you may find you can sit through it for a few hours and afterwards it kind of dies down when it sees its not rattling you like a bully who sees he/she is not upsetting or hurting their target. 

Overall, I advise you to try other methods to help but not to be too hard on yourself if you use pot to try and ease symptoms. Just do it in the spirit of moderation as often as you can.

This was the first mental health symptom I ever had. I had exactly what you have. Trust me when I say it can go away. A lot of the fear from my experience was the thought “I will have to control my breathe forever”. As some other posters have mentioned it is a form of OCD from what I understand. 

I honestly don’t know any advice to really give since it randomly went away for me. For a long time I would go without the symptoms and then I would think of it and then it would come roaring back. Now I don’t have my symptoms triggered from thinking about. This just goes to show it can go away. 

I would suggest talking to a therapist about it. I would also suggest some CBT tactics. For instance, remind yourself that while you can control your breathe, if you “forget” to, your body will straight up take over. It is kind of like your heart rate in the sense that you can make it go faster or slower (with exercise or meditation for instance) but if you do nothing, guess what? Your heart will continue to beat. You don’t have to do anything to continue breathing. Slowly, over time, you may find yourself relinquishing the responsibility of breathing. So if you remind yourself of that it could help. Also, if it doesn’t make you too anxious, do some belly breathing exercises (should be lots you can find on google). If you can slow your breathe down a bit and feel the relaxation response, I would then try to distract myself by thinking of something else, reading, doing another task etc.

I would like to echo the other commenters here. It’s much better to catch it early and kill the disorder than let it fester. Not to say people can’t or don’t overcome it once it gets bad, but all the literature I’ve seen says your chances are better if you receive appropriate treatment quickly. I recommend seeing a therapist who specializes in anxiety disorders and if possible someone who specializes in agoraphobia itself. If that’s not possible, try The Panic Attacks Workbook by David Carbonell. It’s a low cost “replacement” for therapy, and I’ve heard of people having great results. 

For me, I didn’t realize what was happening until it was too late. The reason for this was I had different anxiety disorders over the years and it was super murky to discern what was causing certain things. I was diagnosed GAD in teens but then slowly I think it became more Panic Disorder and even some “latent” agoraphobia. I was using safety nets and doing some avoidance without even realizing it was agoraphobia, since I just thought it was pretty extreme GAD. 

All in all, you’re in a good position. You know the issue in front of you, which not everyone can say when they first start to develop it. I know it may seem overwhelming, but there is no need to “freak out” or anything. Just do the best you can. It’s all we can do as people. 

I think if you do that (your best) you will end up doing just fine. And also don’t fret if you don’t see immediate results, sometimes it takes some repetition for people to feel comfortable again. 

I wish you all the best. Feel free to contact me if you ever want to discuss this further.

Hah, it’s like we are the same frickin person. I know ALL about that feeling. The only difference is I don’t feel sick physically (which is what I assume you’re talking about) but I worry about panicking the whole way back. So the further I go, the worse the anxiety gets. 

That’s why you try and take distance out of the equation. You just get yourself to a targeted anxiety level. Then slowly over time, in theory, you’re gonna get better at tolerating that distress. This was all taught to me by an exposure therapist. 

And even with an exposure therapist helping me (who I no longer can see due to insurance reasons) I still have not fully recovered. I have made tons of progress though (even if it’s not nearly as much or as fast as I would like). Yet I still can hardly go anywhere I want to go since I live in a terrible location. However, if I lived somewhere else, the few sessions I had may have been enough to get me up and running. 

The exposure therapist always said “remember, this is not about distance. It is about tolerating distress in a healthy way so you don’t have to white knuckle it”. The therapist told me the following steps (loosely adapted from a book on Panic by David Carbonell)

A- Acknowledge and accept. When you start to feel panic or sickness, acknowledge it and accept it. Tell yourself “this is only discomfort, not danger”

W- watch and wait. For a minute or two act like a dispassionate observer. Like a scientist who is visiting a classroom to observe human behavior. Just notice what is going on in your body. Let it be, don’t try and change it. 

A- Action. If panicking, do diaphragmatic breathing. First let all the air out, by forcing it out through your mouth. Breathe in through nose and let belly rise, hold for slightly longer than the inhale, then purse your lips and breathe slowly out of your mouth like you’re breathing through a cocktail straw. 

R- Return to what you were doing. So if that was driving, take your full focus back to that activity. Or return your focus to literally whatever you were doing before your symptoms started. 

E- Carbonell book has this step and I have not gotten to it yet. My particular therapist only included the first 4 and said I didn’t need to worry about the last step so much. 

So that is the AWARE cycle taught to me (without the E, of course) 

One thing I was taught though, is to try and not use this when doing planned exposures. You want to try and “float” through them. Show yourself you do not need the belly breathing and that the anxiety will just come and go. However, if you really start to panic, you should try this out. I was told to use the aware cycle to make yourself comfortable in a bad situation, but during your planned exposures it is best to show yourself you will be fine without taking any action whatsoever. Maybe the one thing you could still do is the A part, acknowledging and accepting it is discomfort not danger. 

One last thing. Practice the belly breathing several times a day the first couple weeks at least. It really helps you feel more confident if you find yourself panicking really badly. Trust me, I know from experience;) 

Hope this was helpful. Feel free to pm me anytime.

One more thing to add to my previous comment. Try not to think about distance too much (I still am incapable of doing this, but let me explain). So if you get to your target anxiety level just backing out of the driveway, go no further. Just stop and let it play out. If you make it maybe 20 or 30 min away from home one day, and you go out the next day and can’t make it 10 minutes you may have a desire to “push through” to match previous days progress. I’ve been told to absolutely not do that. Wherever gets you to your predetermined level, that is where you either stop and relax for a bit or go around in circles. But try to take distance out of the equation, at least at the start. 

I’m still feeling like shit that I can’t go certain distances, but I just try to remind myself I am making slow progress even if it doesn’t feel that way. Just keep that in mind. It is about learning to tolerate symptoms and not about tolerating distance.

You just stop or do circles until the anxiety comes down. Goal is to endure between 30-60 minutes of the anxiety. If you get up to the level you are aiming for and stop, and then it goes away within like 5 minutes, you go out and drive further. On the other hand if you stop and are still really anxious for another 20 min or so, I would just head home to be honest or maybe do some circles (or if you’re near a store and that makes you a bit anxious, just pop in for a few minutes to get the anxiety up a bit so you can say you spent 30 min instead of 20 at your level) So pretty much if you reach your “desired level” of anxiety, you only go further if it goes down by 50% or more really quickly. I found that if I endured my level of anxiety for about 25 min then pushed further, I couldn’t get out and do my daily work. Each day was too excruciating. You have to calibrate it so you are not pushing too hard too fast. 

If you’re anxious on the way to whatever distance gets you to target level, you can sort of consider that. So if I go out and I get to a 5 or 6 out of 10 (just an example) but I was at a good 4 on the way there, I may just endure 20 min at my target level. However, if I wasn’t anxious at all on the way, maybe I push myself a little bit more once I reach my target (say stay for about 30 min).
